sections.title: What Spring and Spring Boot Are

blocks.text:
Every non-trivial Java program is a graph of objects that need each other: a controller needs a service, the service needs a repository, the repository needs a data source. In plain Java you build that graph by hand with `new`, and the code that creates objects gets mixed with the code that uses them. Tests become hard (you cannot swap the real database for a fake), and every change to a constructor ripples through the program.

**Spring Framework** solves this with **Inversion of Control (IoC)**: you describe your classes and what they need, and a container creates the objects and hands each one its collaborators. Passing collaborators in from outside is called **dependency injection (DI)**. The objects the container manages are called **beans**. Around that core, Spring offers web (MVC), data access, transactions, security, testing and more.

**Spring Boot** is an opinionated layer on top of Spring Framework. Plain Spring needed pages of XML or Java configuration before the first request could be served. Boot removes that boilerplate with four ideas:

- **Starters**: single dependencies such as `spring-boot-starter-web` that pull in a tested, compatible set of libraries.
- **Auto-configuration**: Boot looks at what is on your classpath and what you defined, and configures sensible defaults (a web server, a JSON mapper, a connection pool) for you.
- **Embedded server**: Tomcat runs inside your application, so you ship one jar and start it with `java -jar`.
- **Production features**: Actuator gives health checks and metrics; externalised configuration lets one jar run in many environments.

blocks.text:
### Version map

Versions move, so check before you start a project. At the time of writing (October 2026) the current Spring Boot release is 4.1.x, built on Spring Framework 7.0.x, and it requires Java 17 or later (it supports up to Java 26). The previous major line, Spring Boot 3.5.x (Spring Framework 6.2), is still widely used in industry and in existing code bases.

rows: Very common in existing projects. Jackson 2 (`com.fasterxml.jackson`).
Current. Modularised starters, Jackson 3 (`tools.jackson`) by default.
blocks.caption: Boot lines you will meet.

blocks.text: This guide writes code that works on both lines. Where they differ you will see a short note. Always confirm exact numbers at spring.io/projects/spring-boot and in the "System Requirements" page of the reference documentation; they change with each release.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Spring Boot 4 and Jackson 3 Jackson 3 moved its packages from `com.fasterxml.jackson` to `tools.jackson` (the annotations module keeps the old package). You only notice this if you import Jackson classes directly, for example a custom serializer. Everything in this guide uses Boot's auto-configured JSON support and never imports Jackson types.

### Creating a project

The standard way is **start.spring.io** (Spring Initializr), also built into IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code. Choose Maven, Java, the latest stable Boot version, a group (`com.example`) and artifact (`library`), packaging Jar, Java 21 (or 17 or 25), and add the dependencies **Spring Web** and **Spring Boot Actuator**. Download the zip and open it. If you cannot reach the site, you can write the files below by hand; they are all it takes.

#### The pom.xml

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
                             https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.1</version> <!-- use the latest 4.x or 3.5.x -->
    <relativePath/>
  </parent>

  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>library</artifactId>
  <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>

  <properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
blocks.title: pom.xml

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- The **parent** `spring-boot-starter-parent` fixes the versions of hundreds of libraries (Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, Tomcat, JUnit...). That is why the dependencies below have no `<version>`: the parent's dependency management supplies a combination that has been tested together.
- A **starter** is just a dependency whose purpose is to drag in the right transitive dependencies. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC, an embedded Tomcat and Jackson.
- The **Spring Boot Maven plugin** builds the executable "fat" jar and provides `spring-boot:run`.
- Under Boot 4 some starters were split into smaller modules (for example, the web starter also exists in a REST-focused form); the plain starters used in this guide still work. If a starter name from an older tutorial fails to resolve, look at the migration guide on the Spring Boot wiki.

#### Project layout

blocks.code:
library/
├── mvnw, mvnw.cmd              Maven wrapper scripts (no Maven install needed)
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/example/library/
    │   │   └── LibraryApplication.java     main class, in the ROOT package
    │   └── resources/
    │       ├── application.properties      configuration
    │       ├── static/                     static files served as-is
    │       └── templates/                  server-side templates (not used in an API)
    └── test/java/com/example/library/
        └── LibraryApplicationTests.java

blocks.text:
Put the main class in the root package of your code (`com.example.library`) and every other class in sub-packages (`...library.book`, `...library.loan`). The reason is component scanning, explained in the next chapter.

#### The first application

blocks.title: LibraryApplication.java

blocks.text:
The three lines of real code do a lot: `@SpringBootApplication` turns on auto-configuration and scanning, `SpringApplication.run` creates the container and starts Tomcat, and `@RestController` plus `@GetMapping` register a web endpoint. The `./mvnw` script is the **Maven wrapper**: it downloads the Maven version the project expects, so nobody needs to install Maven.

#### Building and running the executable jar

blocks.code:
$ ./mvnw clean package
$ ls target/*.jar
target/library-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
$ java -jar target/library-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --server.port=9090
blocks.title: Package and run (typical output)

blocks.text: `package` produces an **executable jar** (often called a fat jar): your classes plus every dependency, including Tomcat, laid out so that Boot's own launcher can start it. One file, one command, no application server to install. Command-line arguments such as `--server.port=9090` override configuration, a topic covered in the configuration chapter.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot? Spring Framework is the core: the IoC container, DI, AOP, MVC, data and transaction support. Spring Boot is a layer that makes Spring quick to use: starters for dependency management, auto-configuration that configures beans from the classpath and properties, an embedded server for self-contained jars, and production features such as Actuator. Boot does not replace Spring; every Boot application is a Spring application.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Mixing Boot versions Do not override the version of a single Spring or Jackson library next to the Boot parent. Mixed versions cause errors such as `NoSuchMethodError` at startup. Change the Boot version and let dependency management follow.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Spring is an IoC container plus libraries; Boot adds starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server and Actuator.
- The Boot parent POM manages library versions; you add starters without versions.
- Put the `@SpringBootApplication` class in the root package.
- `./mvnw spring-boot:run` runs from source; `./mvnw package` plus `java -jar` runs the executable jar.
- Check the current Boot version and Java requirement at spring.io before starting.

sections.title: The Spring Container and Dependency Injection

blocks.text:
### The problem and the idea

Consider a service that needs a repository. Without DI the service builds its own:

`BookService` now knows which implementation to use and how to construct it. You cannot test it with a fake repository, and if `JdbcBookRepository` later needs a `DataSource`, every caller changes. With DI the class only declares what it needs:

The mental picture: a **container** holds a registry of beans. At startup it reads your class definitions, works out the dependency graph, creates each bean in the right order, and passes dependencies into constructors. Your code never calls `new` on a managed class.

### A 40-line container, run on plain Java

To see that there is no magic, here is a toy container. It takes a class, inspects the constructor with reflection, recursively creates the parameter types, and caches each instance (so every bean is a singleton). Real Spring does far more, but this is the core of constructor injection.

blocks.title: MiniDi.java

walkthrough.title: One instance per type
walkthrough.text: The container keeps a cache of instances by type; this is what makes every bean a singleton.

walkthrough.title: Reuse what exists
walkthrough.text: If an instance of the requested type was already created, return it.

walkthrough.title: Inspect the constructor
walkthrough.text: Otherwise, use reflection to find the constructor and its parameter types.

walkthrough.title: Create the dependencies first
walkthrough.text: Each parameter type is created by calling `get` again, recursively.

walkthrough.title: Create, cache, return
walkthrough.text: Call the constructor with the created arguments, remember the instance and return it.

walkthrough.title: Asking for the controller
walkthrough.text: Asking for `BookController` made the container build `BookRepository`, then `BookService`, then the controller.

walkthrough.title: Same instance
walkthrough.text: The second line prints `true`: the service is a single shared instance.

blocks.code:
$ java MiniDi.java
Service says: Book#7
true
blocks.title: Run on JDK 21

blocks.text:
Asking for `BookController` made the container build `BookRepository`, then `BookService`, then the controller, and the second line proves the service is a single shared instance. What this toy lacks: interfaces with several implementations, scopes, configuration, cycles detection, lifecycle callbacks and proxies. Spring has all of them.

### ApplicationContext and beans

The Spring container is the `ApplicationContext` interface (the older, smaller one is `BeanFactory`). `SpringApplication.run` returns it. A **bean** is any object created and managed by it. Spring needs to know which classes are beans; there are two ways to tell it.

#### Stereotype annotations (your own classes)

Put an annotation on the class and component scanning finds it.

rows: Business logic. Same behaviour as `@Component`, but documents intent.
Data access. Also enables translation of persistence exceptions to Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy.
A class that declares beans with `@Bean` methods.
blocks.caption: Stereotypes. All are specialisations of @Component.

blocks.text:
#### @Configuration and @Bean (classes you do not own)

You cannot add `@Component` to a library class such as `Clock`. Instead, write a factory method:

blocks.title: AppConfig.java

blocks.text:
The method name becomes the bean name, the return type is the bean type, and parameters of a `@Bean` method are injected, so one bean can depend on another. Injecting a `Clock` into services (instead of calling `Instant.now()`) also makes time testable.

### Constructor injection

Spring supports three injection styles. Prefer the first.

Field injection (`@Autowired private BookRepository books;`) looks shorter, but the fields cannot be `final`, you cannot construct the class in a unit test without reflection or a Spring context, and the list of dependencies hides inside the class so a class with eight of them does not look wrong. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and mandatory, and a service with too many constructor parameters shows you the design problem. Setter injection is for genuinely optional dependencies.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection? Dependencies can be final and immutable; the object is never half-initialised; it is testable with plain `new` and mocks, no container needed; missing dependencies fail at startup; and a large constructor is a visible hint that a class does too much. Field injection also hides circular dependencies that constructor injection reports immediately.

### More than one candidate: @Primary and @Qualifier

If two beans match a requested type, Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. You resolve the ambiguity in one of two ways.

Without `@Qualifier`, `OverdueService` would get `EmailNotifier` because of `@Primary`. You can also inject `List<Notifier>` to receive all implementations, or `Map<String, Notifier>` keyed by bean name.

### Component scanning rules

`@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan` for the package of the annotated class and everything below it. A `@Service` in `com.example.library.book` is found; one in `com.example.other` is silently ignored and you get a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` for a missing bean at startup. Fix by moving the class (best) or by widening the scan with `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "...")`. Classes without a stereotype annotation (or a `@Bean` method) are not beans.

### Scopes

rows: The default. One shared instance per container.
A new instance every time the bean is requested from the container.
One instance per HTTP request (web applications only).
One instance per HTTP session (web applications only).
blocks.caption: Bean scopes.

blocks.text: Choose a non-singleton scope with `@Scope("prototype")`. Most beans stay singletons: services, repositories and controllers are stateless collaborators, which is what makes sharing safe.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Singletons are shared between threads Tomcat handles many requests at once, all calling the same controller and service instances. A mutable field in a singleton is shared state: `private int counter;` incremented in a service method loses updates under load, and `private SimpleDateFormat fmt;` breaks randomly. Keep singletons stateless (state lives in method variables or in the database), or use thread-safe types such as `AtomicInteger` and `ConcurrentHashMap`. Injecting a prototype bean into a singleton also gives you one instance only (created once at injection), which surprises people; inject an `ObjectProvider<T>` to get a fresh one each time.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The container creates beans and injects dependencies; you declare, it wires.
- Use stereotypes for your classes, `@Bean` methods for third-party types.
- Prefer constructor injection: final fields, testable, explicit.
- `@Primary` and `@Qualifier` resolve several candidates; scanning starts at the main class's package.
- Beans are singletons by default, so keep them stateless or thread-safe.

### From class to usable bean

For each singleton bean the container goes through the same steps. Knowing them explains most "why is this null" and "why did my annotation do nothing" bugs.

blocks.caption: The bean lifecycle: instantiate, inject dependencies, post-processors and init callbacks, use, then destroy callbacks on shutdown.
blocks.alt: Bean creation | Post-process | Instantiate Inject | and init | constructor dependencies | @PostConstruct | In use @PreDestroy | singleton on shutdown

blocks.text:
1. **Instantiate** the object (calls the constructor; constructor dependencies are resolved first).
2. **Populate** properties (setter and field injection, if used).
3. **Aware callbacks** (for example `BeanNameAware`), rarely needed.
4. `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`.
5. **Initialisation**: the method annotated `@PostConstruct`, then `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet`, then a custom `initMethod`.
6. `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization`: this is where proxies are created.
7. The bean is ready and lives until shutdown.
8. **Destruction**: `@PreDestroy`, then `DisposableBean.destroy`, when the context closes.

blocks.title: CacheWarmer.java

walkthrough.title: Instantiate
walkthrough.text: The constructor runs first, with its dependencies resolved. Keep constructors light.

walkthrough.title: @PostConstruct
walkthrough.text: Runs once, after the dependencies are injected.

walkthrough.title: @PreDestroy
walkthrough.text: Runs once on graceful shutdown, when the context closes.

blocks.text:
Note the `jakarta.annotation` package. Since Spring Boot 3 everything moved from `javax.*` to `jakarta.*`; copy-pasting an old `javax.annotation.PostConstruct` import is a classic error.

Prototype beans are only created and initialised by the container; it does not call their destroy callbacks.

### BeanPostProcessor: how Spring adds behaviour

A `BeanPostProcessor` is a bean that sees every other bean after creation and may modify or **replace** it. Many Spring features are post-processors: `@Autowired` handling, `@PostConstruct` handling, and the ones that create proxies for `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable` and method security. You will rarely write one, but you should know that these annotations work through the container, not through the language.

### Proxies: what @Transactional really does

Annotations such as `@Transactional` are only markers. The behaviour is added by wrapping your bean in a **proxy**: an object with the same type that receives each call, does something before (open a transaction), calls your real method, then does something after (commit or roll back).

blocks.title: A call through the proxy
blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant C as caller participant P as proxy
(what the container actually injects) participant R as real LoanService C->>P: call method Note over P: begin tx P->>R: call real method R-->>P: return Note over P: commit / rollback P-->>C: return
blocks.caption: The proxy does something before (open a transaction), calls your real method, then does something after (commit or roll back).

blocks.text:
When another bean receives a `LoanService`, it is really holding the proxy. Spring creates proxies either with the JDK's `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` (when the bean implements interfaces) or with CGLIB, which generates a subclass; Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`). Consequences of the subclass approach: the class and its advised methods cannot be `final`, and the advised method must be `public` (or at least visible to the proxy) to be intercepted.

#### The self-invocation gotcha

walkthrough.title: The outer method
walkthrough.text: `borrowAll` is called through the proxy, but it calls `borrow` on `this`.

walkthrough.title: Direct call
walkthrough.text: `this.borrow(...)` is a direct call: the proxy is bypassed.

walkthrough.title: No transaction
walkthrough.text: `@Transactional` on `borrow` never takes effect when it is called from `borrowAll`.

blocks.title: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy
blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant C as caller participant P as proxy participant R as real LoanService C->>P: borrowAll(ids) P->>R: borrowAll(ids) R->>R: this.borrow(id) Note over R: direct call on the real object,
the proxy is bypassed: no transaction
blocks.caption: A call from one method to another inside the same object uses `this`, which is the real object, so @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable and @PreAuthorize on the second method are silently skipped.

blocks.text: The proxy only intercepts calls that come from outside through it. A call from one method to another inside the same object uses `this`, which is the real object, so `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable` and `@PreAuthorize` on `borrow` are silently skipped. No exception is thrown; the bug shows up as missing rollbacks. Fixes, in order of preference: move the annotated method to another bean and inject it; put the annotation on the outer method; or (last resort) inject the bean into itself.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Annotations that need a proxy fail silently `@Transactional` on a private method, on a `final` method or called through `this` does nothing and reports nothing. If a transaction or async behaviour "does not work", check the call path first, annotation spelling second.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle and how @Transactional works. The container instantiates the bean, injects dependencies, runs BeanPostProcessors and init callbacks (`@PostConstruct`), the bean serves requests, and `@PreDestroy` runs at shutdown. `@Transactional` works through AOP: a post-processor wraps the bean in a proxy that opens a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after it. Because the proxy only sees external calls, self-invocation bypasses the transaction.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Lifecycle: instantiate, inject, post-processors, `@PostConstruct`, use, `@PreDestroy`.
- `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable` work through proxies created by post-processors.
- Self-invocation, `private` and `final` methods bypass the proxy silently.
- Use `jakarta.*` imports in Boot 3 and 4.

Code that is identical in every environment still needs different settings in each: a port, a database URL, a feature flag, a password. Spring Boot's **externalised configuration** lets you keep those values outside the compiled jar so one build runs everywhere.

### application.properties and application.yml

Boot reads `src/main/resources/application.properties` (or `application.yml`) from the classpath. The two formats are equivalent; YAML is more readable for nested keys but is whitespace-sensitive.

blocks.code:
server.port=8080
spring.application.name=library
library.loan-days=14
library.max-loans-per-member=5
logging.level.com.example.library=DEBUG
blocks.title: application.properties

blocks.code:
server:
  port: 8080
spring:
  application:
    name: library
library:
  loan-days: 14
  max-loans-per-member: 5
logging:
  level:
    com.example.library: DEBUG
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
Use one format per project. Boot has hundreds of built-in keys; the "Common Application Properties" appendix of the reference documentation lists them.

### Reading values: @Value and @ConfigurationProperties

#### @Value for one-off values

`@Value` is quick, but strings scattered across classes are easy to mistype, are not validated together, and give no IDE help.

#### @ConfigurationProperties for groups (preferred)

Bind a prefix to a typed object. A Java record works well because it is immutable and Boot binds it through the canonical constructor.

blocks.title: LibraryProperties.java
LibraryApplication.java

blocks.text:
Then inject `LibraryProperties` into any bean like any other dependency. What to notice:

- **Relaxed binding**: `library.loan-days` (kebab case, recommended in files), `library.loanDays` and the environment variable `LIBRARY_LOANDAYS` all bind to `loanDays`.
- With `@Validated` and a Bean Validation implementation on the classpath (`spring-boot-starter-validation`), an invalid value such as `library.loan-days=0` stops the application at startup with a clear message. Failing fast beats failing in production.
- Instead of `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` you can annotate a `@Configuration` class with `@EnableConfigurationProperties(LibraryProperties.class)`.

rows: Best for One or two simple values
blocks.caption: @Value versus @ConfigurationProperties.

blocks.text:
### Profiles

A **profile** is a named set of beans and properties that is active only in some environments. Per-profile files are `application-dev.properties`, `application-prod.properties`; they are loaded on top of the base file when the profile is active.

blocks.code:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:library
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example.library=DEBUG
blocks.title: application-dev.properties

blocks.text: Activate profiles with `spring.profiles.active=dev` in a file, with the environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`, or on the command line: `java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod`. Beans can be restricted too:

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Keep prod-only settings out of the base file Put safe defaults for local development in `application.properties`, and override in `application-prod.properties` or, better, with environment variables supplied by the platform. Never rely on a profile name to protect something dangerous such as `ddl-auto=create`.

### Environment variables and the command line

Any property can be given from outside. Environment variables use upper-case with underscores (the dot becomes `_`, a dash is dropped or turned into `_`): `SERVER_PORT=9090`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/library`. This is the normal way containers receive configuration.

blocks.code:
$ SERVER_PORT=9090 java -jar target/library.jar
$ java -jar target/library.jar --server.port=9091 --library.loan-days=21
blocks.title: Override configuration from outside (typical)

blocks.text:
### Property precedence

When the same key appears in several places, the higher source wins. Condensed from the reference documentation, from highest to lowest priority:

1. Test properties (`@SpringBootTest(properties=...)`, `@TestPropertySource`).
2. Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9091`).
3. `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON` and Java system properties (`-Dserver.port=9092`).
4. OS environment variables.
5. Profile-specific files outside the jar, then inside the jar (`application-prod.properties`).
6. Plain `application.properties` outside the jar, then inside the jar.
7. `@PropertySource` annotations and application defaults (`SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties`).

Check the exact and complete ordering in "Externalized Configuration" in the reference before relying on a corner case such as a config import. The rule of thumb is enough for work: the closer to the running process, the stronger. An external file placed next to the jar (or `./config/application.properties`) overrides the one packaged inside.

### Secrets

Never commit passwords, API keys or JWT signing keys to `application.properties` in Git. Provide them at runtime as environment variables, container secrets, or from a secrets manager (Vault, a cloud provider's service, Kubernetes Secrets), and reference them with a placeholder: `spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}`. Remember that Actuator's `env` endpoint can expose configuration; keys with words such as `password`, `secret`, `key` and `token` are masked by default, but do not depend on that as your only protection.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you manage configuration across environments in Spring Boot? Keep one artefact. Base defaults live in `application.properties`; environment-specific values come from profile files, environment variables or command-line arguments, in that rising order of priority. Group settings with `@ConfigurationProperties` (validated) instead of scattered `@Value`s, and keep secrets out of the repository, supplying them at runtime.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Configuration lives outside the code: files, environment variables, command line.
- Prefer `@ConfigurationProperties` records (validated) to loose `@Value`s.
- Profiles select per-environment files and beans; activate with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`.
- Precedence: tests, command line, system properties, environment, profile files, base files.
- Secrets come from the runtime environment, never from Git.

Auto-configuration is the feature that makes Boot feel like magic: add a dependency and a working set of beans appears. It is not magic, it is ordinary Spring `@Configuration` classes that are switched on by conditions. Understanding it lets you debug "why is this bean here" and "why is this bean missing".

blocks.text: ### What @SpringBootApplication really is

So `@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations in one. `@EnableAutoConfiguration` loads the list of auto-configuration classes from every jar on the classpath. Each jar that provides some lists them in a text file:

**META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports**

blocks.code:
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
com.example.hello.HelloAutoConfiguration

blocks.text:
(One fully qualified class name per line. The older `spring.factories` mechanism was replaced by this file in Boot 2.7/3.0. In Boot 4 the framework's own auto-configurations were split into per-technology modules, so some built-in class names and packages differ from older tutorials, but the file name and the mechanism are the same.)

### Conditions

An auto-configuration class is guarded by conditional annotations. The most important:

rows: a class is on the classpath (the library was added)
a bean of that type already exists
no such bean exists: the application's own definition always wins
a property has a given value (feature flags)
the app is a web application
blocks.caption: Common conditions.

blocks.text:
`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is the key to Boot's "back off" behaviour. Boot defines a default `ObjectMapper`, `DataSource` or `RestClient.Builder` only if you have not declared your own. To customise something, you therefore usually declare a bean of the same type and Boot steps aside.

### Seeing what happened: the conditions report

Run with `--debug` (or `debug=true` in properties). Boot prints the **conditions evaluation report**.

blocks.code:
$ java -jar target/library.jar --debug
============================
CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT
============================

Positive matches:
-----------------
   WebMvcAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'jakarta.servlet.Servlet', ...

Negative matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'javax.sql.DataSource' ...
blocks.title: Print the report (typical output, shortened)

blocks.text:
Positive matches say what was configured and why, negative matches say what was not and which condition failed. When you ask "why is there no `DataSource`?" the answer is in the negative section, typically a missing dependency. With Actuator on the classpath, the `/actuator/conditions` endpoint shows the same information.

### Excluding auto-configuration

Sometimes you want to turn one off: for example, a project that has a JDBC driver on the classpath but does not want Boot to create a `DataSource` yet.

blocks.code:
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class LibraryApplication { /* ... */ }

blocks.text:
or in properties: `spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration` (use the class name that matches your Boot version; check the conditions report for the exact name).

### Starters: what they are and are not

A starter contains no logic. It is a dependency descriptor (a pom) that pulls in a library together with its Boot auto-configuration and compatible companions. The rule: **starter = dependencies, auto-configuration =** **behaviour.** Naming: official starters are `spring-boot-starter-xyz`; third-party ones should be `xyz-spring-boot-starter`.

rows: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, a connection pool (HikariCP)
blocks.caption: Starters used in this guide.

blocks.text:
### Writing a tiny auto-configuration

The mechanism is easiest to remember after building it once. Imagine a shared library that offers a `Greeter` bean to any application that adds it. (Spring dependencies required; not run here.)

blocks.title: HelloProperties.java
HelloAutoConfiguration.java
Greeter.java

blocks.text: Register it by adding one line (`com.example.hello.HelloAutoConfiguration`) to `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` in the library's `src/main/resources`. Any application with that jar gets a `Greeter`; setting `hello.greeting=Hi` changes it, `hello.enabled=false` removes it, and declaring its own `Greeter` bean replaces it. Note that auto-configuration classes must not be found by the application's component scan; that is why they are listed in the imports file and live in a separate package.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Why you rarely write one Inside a single application you just use `@Configuration` and `@ConditionalOnProperty` directly. Writing a real auto-configuration is for shared libraries and starters; the mechanism matters mostly so you can read Boot's own and debug it.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work? `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (part of `@SpringBootApplication`) reads the list of candidate configuration classes from `META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports` in every jar on the classpath. Each class is a normal `@Configuration` guarded by conditions such as `@ConditionalOnClass` (the library is present), `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (you have not defined your own) and `@ConditionalOnProperty`. Only the classes whose conditions pass are applied. You inspect the result with `--debug` and customise by defining your own bean, by properties or by `exclude`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Auto-configuration and your own bean definitions If you define a bean and your version is ignored, check the type and name carefully: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` backs off only for a bean of the matching type. If an auto-configured bean you did not expect appears, find the dependency that pulled it in with `./mvnw dependency:tree`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `@SpringBootApplication` = configuration + auto-configuration + component scan.
- Auto-configuration classes are listed in `AutoConfiguration.imports` and guarded by `@Conditional...` annotations.
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` lets your own beans override Boot's defaults.
- `--debug` prints the conditions report; use `exclude` to switch a class off.
- Starters bundle dependencies; they add no behaviour themselves.

#### What Spring and Spring Boot Are

items.question: Name the four ideas that make Boot "opinionated Spring".
items.answer: Starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server, and production features (Actuator, externalised configuration).

items.question: Why do the dependencies in the pom above carry no `<version>`?
items.answer: The `spring-boot-starter-parent` parent supplies dependency management, a tested set of versions.

items.question: Where must the class with `@SpringBootApplication` live, and why?
items.answer: In the root package of the application, because component scanning starts at that package and covers its sub-packages.

items.question: What is inside an executable jar that is not in a normal jar?
items.answer: All the dependency jars (nested) plus Boot's launcher classes, so `java -jar` works with no extra classpath.

items.question: You run `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090`. Which port does Tomcat use if `application.properties` says 8081?
items.answer: 9090: command-line arguments have higher precedence than `application.properties`.

blocks.text: #### The Spring Container and Dependency Injection

items.question: What does the code below do on startup, assuming both classes are scanned? `@Component class A { A(B b) {}` `}` and `@Component class B { B(A a) {} }`
items.answer: Startup fails with `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` (a circular dependency through constructors). Break the cycle by redesigning, for example extracting a third class.

items.question: Two beans implement `Notifier` and neither is marked `@Primary`. What happens and how do you fix it?
items.answer: `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Mark one `@Primary`, or inject with `@Qualifier("name")`, or inject a `List<Notifier>`.

items.question: Your `@Service` class is in a package that is a sibling of the main class's package. Is it a bean?
items.answer: No: scanning covers only the main class's package and below. Move it or set `scanBasePackages`.

items.question: A singleton service has `private List<String> cache = new ArrayList<>();` that every request adds to. What is wrong?
items.answer: `ArrayList` is not thread-safe and the state is shared by all requests, so there are data races. Make the service stateless or use a thread-safe structure or external store.

items.question: When do you write a `@Bean` method instead of using `@Component`?
items.answer: For classes you do not control (library types) or when construction needs custom logic or parameters.

blocks.text: #### Bean Lifecycle and Proxies

items.question: In which order run the constructor, `@PostConstruct` and field injection?
items.answer: Constructor, then field/setter injection, then `@PostConstruct`.

items.question: Why does `@Transactional` on a method called by another method of the same class not start a transaction?
items.answer: The call goes through `this`, bypassing the proxy that opens the transaction.

items.question: What goes wrong with this: `@Transactional public final void save()`?
items.answer: A CGLIB proxy cannot override a final method, so the advice does not apply (no transaction).

items.question: Which package is `PostConstruct` in on Spring Boot 3 and 4?
items.answer: `jakarta.annotation`.

items.question: A prototype-scoped bean has a `@PreDestroy` method. Will it run at shutdown?
items.answer: No. The container does not manage the destruction of prototype beans.

blocks.text: #### Configuration

items.question: `application.properties` has `server.port=8080` and you start with `SERVER_PORT=9090 java -jar app.jar` `--server.port=9091`. Which port wins?
items.answer: 9091: command-line arguments beat environment variables.

items.question: Why might `library.loan-days=0` crash the app at startup in the example above?
items.answer: `@Min(1)` on the record with `@Validated` fails binding validation, so the context fails fast.

items.question: What is wrong here? `@Value("${library.loan-days}") private int days;` where the key is absent from all sources.
items.answer: No default is given, so startup fails with an unresolved placeholder error. Use `${library.loan-days:14}` or a properties record with `@DefaultValue`.

items.question: How do you activate the `prod` profile in a Docker container without changing the image?
items.answer: Set the environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` on the container.

items.question: Name one reason to prefer a record with `@ConfigurationProperties` over several `@Value` fields.
items.answer: Type safety, grouping, validation at startup and immutability (one place to see all settings).

blocks.text: #### Auto-Configuration and Starters

items.question: Name the three annotations that make up `@SpringBootApplication`.
items.answer: `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, `@ComponentScan`.

items.question: Where does Boot find the list of auto-configuration classes?
items.answer: In `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` files inside the jars on the classpath.

items.question: You define your own `ObjectMapper` bean. Why does Boot's default one not appear?
items.answer: Boot's definition is guarded by `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, so it backs off.

items.question: How do you find out why a `DataSource` bean was not created?
items.answer: Start with `--debug` and read the negative matches (or `/actuator/conditions`); the usual cause is a missing dependency or property.

items.question: What is the difference between a starter and an auto-configuration?
items.answer: A starter is a dependency bundle with no logic; auto-configuration is the conditional configuration code that creates the beans.
